name: Beth Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign. Your words are confidential, so please separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. What is an ordinary working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead the developers who maintain payroll software for small firms. I read the overnight error reports, check changes before a release, and take calls when someone's pay is wrong. I like the precision; a decimal point can be someone's grocery money. I have a master's degree, and I've earned this senior role, though a long release day wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home and in the local job market?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband repairs electrical equipment, and we rent a flat near his family. My pay is normal for this job and we've saved about four months of expenses, but we hope to buy a place one day. There are a few other software employers nearby. I use an AI tool now and then, once someone has shown it works on our own cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to use the code helper on repetitive test writing, then check every pay calculation ourselves. Payroll isn't where I want a shortcut that nobody can explain. A little time saved is welcome.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our work and my husband's income would hold up. Four months saved gives us room if a release goes badly or a client leaves. The house deposit might grow slowly, but I wouldn't call that a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep signing off payroll changes and let the helper draft simple tests after a developer checks its results. Starting this month, we'd keep our usual transfer to the house account. In the first year I'd review whether the helper actually reduces errors before giving it more work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My day still has hard deadlines, yet the bills are covered and I have people to ask for help if I get stuck. I can judge this tool by its results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop using the helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it missed a holiday-pay rule in our trial, I'd stop using it on that calculation. A saved hour isn't worth shorting a worker. I'd show the team the failed example rather than argue about AI in general.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you mean by people to ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband and his sister live close, and we trade practical help. I wouldn't ask them to fund a house deposit. We can keep saving at our own pace.

say: I'd use the **code helper** on simple tests while people check every payroll calculation.
I'd welcome **time saved** only when our own trials show the tool does not add pay errors.
think: I expect my **job and household income** to hold up under modest change.
Our **four-month buffer** lets the house deposit grow slowly without putting rent at risk.
do: Keep **signing off payroll changes** before each release.
Continue our **house-account transfer** and review helper errors before giving it more tasks.
feel: **Calm** about work and bills, despite the usual pressure of payroll deadlines.
S0.quote: A saved hour isn't worth shorting a worker.
fieldNote: Her cautious use of AI reflects **payroll responsibility**, with a concrete holiday-pay failure as her stop point.
Typical wages and **four months saved** support a calm mood despite a distant house goal.
Family nearby offers **practical help**, but she does not treat them as money for a deposit.

steps.text: Keep signing off payroll calculations before each software release
Continue monthly transfers into the household house account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should check the tools against real payroll mistakes before promising clients a cheaper service. AI could write routine code and answer simple calls, so junior openings may be the first thing to go. I'd argue for keeping an apprentice route into the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be asked to manage a smaller team and approve far more machine-written work. I know the product well, but if the firm needs fewer developers, my salary could still be cut. Free markets don't promise any one job stays put.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I'd ask for a three-month trial on routine code, with every incorrect pay result logged. I'd take the firm's short course on checking AI output if they pay for it and give me work time. In the first year, if our hours fall, my husband and I would postpone buying a home and pause the house deposit transfer, and I'd apply to the two nearby payroll firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can learn the checking work, and a few local firms hire developers. Still, I lie awake picturing a smaller team with the same responsibility for every pay slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the newest developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to sit with me on a real pay dispute every Friday, even if AI wrote the fix. Somebody has to understand why a worker is short. She shouldn't learn only from neat examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You favour the market, yet want an apprentice place protected. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the case to our manager that trained people catch costly errors. I can't ask a company to keep a place forever for charity. I can show what the apprentice saves us when a client calls angry.

say: I'd demand **real payroll tests** before selling clients an AI-driven price cut.
I'd argue for an **apprentice route** so new developers learn real pay disputes.
think: I could face a **salary cut** if AI lets the firm run payroll with fewer developers.
I know a **market economy** cannot promise my current job will last.
do: Ask for a **three-month trial** that logs wrong pay results starting next week.
Take a **paid AI-checking course** if my employer funds it and gives work time.
Postpone our **home purchase** and apply to nearby payroll firms if paid hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about team cuts and pay responsibility, though she has some local alternatives.
S1.quote: Free markets don't promise any one job stays put.
fieldNote: Her market outlook does not erase **personal job risk** or her concern for apprentices.
She would learn checking skills only with **funded work time**, protecting the household budget.
The postponed **home purchase** and local applications are conditional on lost hours, not immediate actions.

steps.text: Take employer-funded AI checking course during paid work time
Postpone buying a home and pause deposit transfers if paid hours fall
Apply to two nearby payroll software firms if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff that AGI by 2028 threatens our coding and checking work right away. Robots around 2031 have little to do with our desks. I would ask for honest notice of any cuts and a way for clients to challenge wrong pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my developer team's work could be bought more cheaply, even the hard reviews. My husband still has hands-on repair work for a while, but software handles his bookings, and robots may reach physical repairs later. Four months saved isn't enough to carry our rent for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'd list our essential monthly bills with my husband and move part of the house deposit into an emergency account. I'd ask my manager for a reference and for paid time to learn payroll operations beyond code. In the first year after 2028, if I'm laid off, I'd apply to local payroll support teams and take a paid operations role while training in bookkeeping only if the course is affordable without missing rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I believe in getting back to work, but two years would not give us a second trade and a larger cushion. I worry about losing my wage before we have either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your husband's family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband's sister that we're putting the house plan on hold, not asking her to pay our bills. She could tell me whether any small firm needs payroll help. I'd rather ask for a lead than pretend I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must a bookkeeping course cost for you to take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare its fee with our rent buffer after a job offer or layoff. I won't empty the emergency account for a certificate with no paid opening in sight. I'd ask employers what training they actually require.

say: I'd ask for **honest layoff notice** as thinking AI reaches payroll software by 2028.
I'd insist clients retain a way to **challenge wrong pay** after AGI takes over reviews.
think: I expect my **developer wage** could go, even though my husband has hands-on repair work for now.
Our **four months saved** cannot replace years of rent if coding work disappears.
do: Postpone the **home purchase**, move deposit money into emergency savings, and list essential bills tomorrow.
Seek **paid payroll operations training** and a manager reference while still employed.
Apply for **local payroll support** after layoff; study bookkeeping only if fees leave rent covered and vacancies require it.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected loss of her wage before a second trade or larger cushion is ready.
S2.quote: Four months saved isn't enough to carry our rent for years.
fieldNote: She knows robots follow around **2031**, but her own coding exposure arrives with thinking AI in 2028.
Her husband's repair income helps temporarily, without making **household rent** secure if her wage ends.
Bookkeeping study requires **affordability** and **paid openings**; she refuses to spend the emergency account blindly.

steps.text: Postpone buying a home and move deposit money into emergency savings
Study bookkeeping if fees leave rent covered and paid vacancies require it
Apply for local payroll support jobs if laid off after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team five years lets us teach apprentices how payroll really works while we still have jobs. I'd ask our company to publish a yearly staffing plan, because waiting until 2031 would waste the warning. Physical robots arriving about 2034 won't delay our screen work changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build enough savings and payroll experience to move into a client-facing role by then. I still don't know if a firm will pay people to explain pay errors when AGI can explain them too. I need a real vacancy, not a reassuring title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This quarter I'd put a fixed share of each pay cheque into an emergency account until it holds six months of expenses. I'd ask to sit with the payroll support team twice a month and enroll in their paid in-house training if my manager approves it. In the first year after 2031, if developer hours shrink and support jobs exist, I'd apply there before leaving the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less frightened than with two years. Five years could let me do the training and keep our rent buffer intact. I would still watch each staffing plan closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on those support days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit through a call about a missed shift allowance, then trace the number back through our software. I'd ask the support lead to let me explain the correction on the next call. I need to hear how people describe a bad pay day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your manager refuses the training time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the written reasons and enroll in a short evening course only if its fee fits our budget and nearby payroll roles require it. My husband and I would decide that together.

say: I'd call for a **yearly staffing plan** and payroll apprenticeships before 2031.
I'd remind colleagues that **2034 robots** do not postpone our screen-based disruption.
think: I could build a **six-month cushion** and learn client-facing payroll work over five years.
I need an **actual vacancy**, since AGI might also explain pay errors cheaply.
do: Save a **fixed pay share** until the emergency account holds six months of expenses.
Enroll in **paid support training** if approved, or an affordable required course if it is refused.
Apply for **payroll support** if developer hours shrink and paid openings exist after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about future income, with time to gain relevant experience and preserve rent money.
S3.quote: I need a real vacancy, not a reassuring title.
fieldNote: Her plan tests **payroll support** through real calls about missed allowances, rather than treating it as abstract retraining.
She sets a **six-month target** before counting on a job move.
Both training and transfer depend on **approval, affordability or vacancies** stated in her answers.

steps.text: Transfer a fixed pay share until emergency savings cover six months
Enroll in paid payroll support training if the manager approves it
Enroll in an affordable evening payroll course if paid training is refused and vacancies require it
Apply for paid payroll support vacancies if developer hours shrink after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger developers to learn the rules behind payroll and spend time with the people who get paid. Ten years means I can build experience and savings without panicking. I'd still ask the company how it expects to employ people after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband and I could have a home deposit and a fuller emergency account by my late thirties. That's a possibility, not a promise; a bad year at either job could interrupt it. Coding itself might pay less after 2036, so I'd want skills a payroll client actually buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd keep the house transfer but increase the emergency account to six months first. I'd take a formal payroll administration course only if nearby vacancies ask for it, the fees fit after rent and my employer won't offer paid training. In the first year after 2036, if developer jobs contract, I'd apply for paid payroll administration posts before resigning; if none exist, I'd keep whichever paid work I still have and reassess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The long runway makes a plan possible, and our present pay and savings are sound. I dislike imagining that careful coding becomes a skill employers barely buy, but it doesn't keep me awake tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would buying a home still be the aim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after the emergency fund reaches six months. I won't use the rent buffer as a deposit just to say we own a place. My husband agrees that the roof comes before the deed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask someone doing payroll administration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask how many disputes they handle in a week and which ones need a person in the room. I'd ask what training led to their paid post. If nobody can point to a vacancy, I won't borrow for a course.

say: I'd urge new developers to learn **payroll rules** and speak with workers about real errors.
I'd ask for an **employment forecast** beyond 2036 rather than assume code remains valuable.
think: I could have a **home deposit** and deeper savings by my late thirties if both incomes hold.
I expect **coding pay** may weaken after 2036, so payroll clients must value any new skill.
do: Grow the **emergency fund** to six months before adding to our home deposit.
Enroll in **payroll administration study** only if vacancies require it, rent remains covered and paid training is unavailable.
Apply for **paid payroll posts** if developer jobs contract after 2036; keep current paid work if no vacancy exists.
feel: **Uneasy** about long-term coding pay, while current work and money feel secure.
S4.quote: I won't use the rent buffer as a deposit just to say we own a place.
fieldNote: She ranks a **six-month emergency fund** above buying a home, despite the longer runway.
Formal study has **three gates**: required by vacancies, affordable after rent, and no paid training available.
She would apply before resigning and retain **paid work** if payroll vacancies do not exist.

steps.text: Build emergency savings to six months before increasing the home deposit
Enroll in payroll study if vacancies require it, rent stays covered and paid training is unavailable
Apply for paid payroll administration posts if developer jobs contract after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Payroll coding and checking could disappear before I have a second trade, and the later robots don't postpone that. Honest layoff notice, paid payroll training, and a real list of local vacancies would help me more than a vague promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who answers a worker when the pay is wrong. Our clients might accept a cheap system, but a person still needs to hear the complaint and take responsibility. I would want that named in every contract.

headlineQuote: Our clients might accept a cheap system, but a person still needs to hear the complaint and take responsibility.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old senior developer** with a master's degree, leading payroll software work for small firms.
Typical pay, a husband's repair income and **four months saved** make her secure today, with some local developer options.
She uses AI **cautiously**, checking its payroll results and defending practical apprenticeship.
The **2028 shock** alarms her because coding and checking could vanish before she gains another paid skill.
With more time, she builds a **rent-safe buffer** and studies payroll administration only against real job requirements.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her coding and checking wage before she can gain another trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest layoff notice**, paid payroll training and a real list of local vacancies would help her.
